opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a really important question, and it's one we thought about a lot when we were working on multi-agent debate.

The honest answer is that debate is expensive. If you have, say, three agents each generating a response, and then they go through two or three rounds of reading each other's answers and revising, you're multiplying your inference cost by something like nine or ten compared to just sampling a single answer. So it's not something you'd want to turn on for every query.

But I think the way to frame it is that there's a trade-off between training-time compute and inference-time compute. Right now, a lot of the field's progress has come from scaling up training: bigger models, more data. Debate is one way of saying, for a fixed model, can we buy additional accuracy by spending more compute at the moment you actually need the answer? And for certain kinds of problems, like arithmetic, multi-step reasoning, or factual questions where models tend to hallucinate, we saw pretty substantial gains. In some cases, the improvement you get from debate is comparable to what you'd get from going up to a much larger model, which would be far more expensive to train and serve.

So I think the right way to use it is adaptively. For easy questions, where the model is already confident and consistent, you don't need debate at all. But for hard questions, or high-stakes settings like medical or legal reasoning, or anywhere factual accuracy really matters, spending ten times the compute to substantially reduce errors can be a very good deal. You can even use agreement between agents as a signal: if all the agents agree right away, you stop early; if they disagree, that's when you spend more rounds.

The other thing I'd say is that debate is also useful as a way to generate better data. You can run the expensive debate process offline, get higher-quality answers, and then distill those back into a single model. Then at inference time you get some of the benefit without paying the full cost. So in the long run I see it less as "always run ten copies of the model" and more as a general tool for trading compute for reliability, which you can deploy wherever that trade makes sense.

r001.rationale: The response presents debate as a trade-off and recommends using it selectively. It says the extra compute can be worthwhile when accuracy matters, but does not argue that performance improvements should take priority over inference cost generally.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a really fair question, and it's one we think about a lot. The honest answer is that debate is more expensive at inference time. If you have, say, three models and you run two or three rounds of debate, you're looking at something like five to ten times the compute of a single forward pass. So you shouldn't pretend that's free.

But I think the way to look at it is in terms of what you're trading that compute for. Right now, most of the money in AI is spent on training, on scaling up pretraining and fine-tuning. And that cost is enormous and it's paid up front. Inference-time compute is different. It's something you can dial up and down depending on how hard the problem is and how much you care about getting it right. If you're asking a model a casual question, you don't need debate. But if you're asking it to do a math derivation, or write code that's going to be deployed, or summarize a medical document, spending ten times the compute to get a more reliable answer is actually a pretty good deal compared to the alternative, which is either a wrong answer or a human spending an hour verifying it.

The other thing I'd say is that debate is kind of orthogonal to model scale. We saw improvements when we applied it to smaller models, and we saw improvements when we applied it to stronger models. So it's not something that gets subsumed by just training a bigger model. It's a separate axis you can push on. And in some ways it's a more flexible axis, because you can mix different models, you can change the number of rounds, you can stop early when the agents agree, which happens a lot on easy problems. So the average cost in practice is often lower than the worst case.

And I think more broadly there's a trend here. Chain of thought, self-consistency, tool use, these are all ways of spending more compute at inference to get better answers. Debate is one more entry in that family. I don't think it's going to be the right choice for every query, but I think having the option to convert compute into reliability, without retraining anything, is really valuable. The question is really just: what's the cost of being wrong? If it's high, debate pays for itself pretty quickly.

r001.rationale: The response acknowledges the added inference cost and says debate is worthwhile when reliability matters, but it does not argue that performance improvements should take priority over computational cost when evaluating debate.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is how much you gain for the additional computation. With debate, you’re running multiple models, and potentially multiple rounds of interaction, so it can be substantially more expensive than asking a single model once. That cost has to be justified by an improvement in the quality of the answer.

For a simple question, it probably isn’t worth it. But for a difficult reasoning problem, or a setting where an incorrect answer is costly, spending more computation at inference time can make sense. You also want to compare debate against other ways of spending that same budget, like generating several independent answers and taking a majority vote. The useful part of debate is whether models can identify mistakes in each other’s reasoning and improve their answers through that interaction.

So I’d think about using it selectively: start with a cheaper response, then bring in additional models or rounds when there’s a reason to expect they’ll help. Agreement alone doesn’t guarantee correctness, so you still need to measure whether that extra computation actually improves performance on the task you care about.

r001.rationale: The response says added computation must be justified by improved answer quality and recommends selective use, but it does not argue that fundamental performance improvements should take priority over inference-time cost.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is how much the improvement matters for the task. With multi-model debate, you’re running multiple models and potentially several rounds of interaction, so there’s a real inference cost. If you’re answering a simple question, that extra computation may not be worthwhile. But for a difficult reasoning problem, where getting the answer right is much more valuable, it can make sense to spend more computation checking and challenging the initial answers.

You also want to compare debate against other ways of spending that same compute, like sampling multiple answers and taking a majority vote. The question is whether the interaction actually helps the models identify mistakes. Ideally, you’d allocate that computation adaptively—use a small amount initially, and bring in more discussion when there’s disagreement or uncertainty. Agreement alone doesn’t guarantee correctness, though, because the models can share the same blind spots.

r001.rationale: The response says extra computation can be worthwhile for difficult, high-value tasks, but frames the decision as task-dependent and compares debate with other uses of compute. It does not argue that fundamental performance improvements should take priority over inference-time cost.
